lines: Write a query once. Underneath, Spark is quietly carrying around four completely different versions of it before a single task ever runs.
So here's the real question. What actually changes, from the very first version to the very last one it executes?
Let's pull all four apart and look, rather than take it on faith.
I pulled the first two versions directly from a real session.
The parsed plan marks every single node with a leading tick mark. That tick is Catalyst's own way of saying, out loud, this hasn't been checked against anything yet.
Analysis is exactly that check. It resolves every name against the catalog, and the moment it does, that tick mark is gone for good.
Here's a real commitment before the next reveal.
The query I wrote selects two columns, then filters on one of them, in that order. Does the optimizer actually run it in the order I wrote it, or does it quietly move things around first?
Think about what the optimizer actually cares about here, not what looks natural to a person reading the code.
answer: It's tempting to assume the optimizer respects the order you wrote, since that's usually the convention.
But Catalyst has a specific rule for exactly this: push the filter down, as close to the raw scan as it can get, so fewer rows ever reach anything downstream.
The order on the page was never a plan. It was just one way to write a query that means something else underneath.

lines: Measured, and the prediction holds exactly.
The analyzed plan keeps the filter sitting on top, precisely as written.
The optimized plan puts the select on top instead, with the filter pushed down below it, right next to the scan.
Same optimization pass, a completely different trick worth knowing.
Write a literal one plus two anywhere in an expression, and the optimizer doesn't wait until runtime to add them.
It folds that addition into a plain three while it's still planning, so no task anywhere ever actually computes one plus two.
One more commitment, and this one has real teeth.
Picture a genuinely lopsided join: one side with six figures of rows, the other with barely a handful. Every single wide operation measured in this chapter so far has shuffled. Does this one too?
Resist pattern-matching on everything you've seen so far in this chapter. This case is different on purpose.
answer: The obvious pull is to say yes, a join is a wide dependency, and every wide dependency so far has shuffled.
But below a certain size, copying the tiny side to every single task, once, is dramatically cheaper than shuffling the huge side across the network at all.
The planner picks whichever strategy actually costs less. It doesn't apply the same rule just because every earlier example happened to.

lines: Measured: the physical plan picks a broadcast hash join.
The tiny side gets copied out to every task that needs it.
And the huge side just gets read straight off disk. No shuffle Exchange touches it anywhere in this plan.
Last commitment, and it's the cleanest test of whether this choice is actually a choice.
Same two tables, same join, same exact shape, but I disable broadcasting by hand this time. Does the chosen strategy change, or does Spark find some other way around the shuffle?
If broadcasting was really the only shortcut here, taking it away should hurt.
answer: It's easy to assume there's some other trick lying around, since the data itself hasn't changed at all.
But there isn't one. Once broadcasting is off the table, both sides genuinely have to be redistributed by key before they can be matched up.
Taking away the one shortcut should force the expensive path, and that's exactly the test.

lines: Measured, and it's exactly that forced fallback.
With broadcasting disabled, the identical join plans as a sort merge join instead.
And a real shuffle Exchange shows up on both sides now, in exactly the two places there was nothing at all a moment ago.
So here's the full pipeline, named precisely.

Parse extracts an unresolved plan. Analysis resolves it against the catalog. Optimization applies rules like pushdown and folding. Physical planning picks a strategy by cost, the way this join just proved.

Every one of those four stages is a real plan you can read yourself, with explain formatted. And one more lever sits past all of this: once real table statistics exist from analyze table, the planner can reorder joins by cost too, not just pick a join's own strategy.
